paragraphs: Friend, this passage is a lesson in what to do when life piles on. David is running from his own son, and on the road he gets a convenient story from Ziba and a mouthful of curses from Shimei. Notice what David does with the first one. He hands over everything Mephibosheth owns after hearing only one side (2 Samuel 16:3-4). I think that's what happens when we're worn out: we decide fast, and fast isn't always wise.

Now look at the second one, because this is the heart of it. Shimei throws stones and yells, and Abishai wants to cut off his head (2 Samuel 16:9). David says, "Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the LORD has told him so" (2 Samuel 16:11). I think David is stunned and hurting, but he doesn't hit back. He puts his hope in God instead: "Perhaps the LORD will see my affliction and repay me with good for the cursing I receive today" (2 Samuel 16:12).

So here's what I want you to carry out of my bakery, baker. When you're hurting, you can slow down before you answer, and you can hand the hurt to God before you hand out payback. He sees affliction, and you don't have to be the one to settle every score. David ends the day exhausted, and he refreshes himself (2 Samuel 16:14). The story isn't over, and neither is the way God uses a hard day.
